L706@P18: 5. These reforms have been largely effective in containing the wage bill, with the
L707@P18: education and health sectors contributing the most (Figure 1). In 2010–2015, the wage bill was
L708@P18: reduced by 2.4 percentage points of GDP, and contributed to more than two-thirds of total
L709@P18: expenditure consolidation (-3.5 percentage points of GDP). 3 As a result, the wage bill appears within
L710@P18: the range of other European countries and slightly above the euro area average as a percent of GDP
L711@P18: (Figure 1b). Health and education, which employ the largest number of public employees,
L712@P18: contributed 25 and 45 percent, respectively, of the total wage bill consolidation. However, wage
L713@P18: spending in these sectors remains higher than the euro area average, by about 0.4 percent of GDP
L714@P18: in education and 0.6 percent of GDP in health (Figure 1c).

L723@P19: 6. In the education sector, efficiency improved during the adjustment program. The
L724@P19: student-teacher ratio increased significantly in both primary and secondary education, while it
L725@P19: declined in tertiary education (Figure 2). The average size class also rose from 2010-2014, both in
L726@P19: primary (from 20.1 to 22.1 pupils per class) and secondary education (from 21.2 to 22.7), and is now
L727@P19: above the EU average. But average annual teaching hours have declined in primary education,
L728@P19: possibly driven by ageing teachers who have reduced teaching hour obligations (but higher nonteaching hours),4 and remain relatively low in secondary education (Figure 3). Overall, Portugal
L729@P19: appears better positioned in primary education compared to other European countries, but
L730@P19: significant efficiency gains have been achieved in the secondary education as well, with lower
L731@P19: spending per student associated with higher PISA score (Figure 4).

L898@P22: 7. In the health sector, various indicators point to further room for efficiency gains
L899@P22: (Figure 5). Benchmarking public employment in the health sector is difficult, reflecting differences
L900@P22: in accounting for spending on wages of primary doctors and nurses across countries. Overall,
L901@P22: Portugal appears to have a higher ratio of doctors relative to the euro area average and most
L902@P22: comparators, with a sharper increase since 2008. Progress was achieved during the adjustment
L903@P22: program in shifting doctors from hospital services to primary care, an effective way in reducing
L904@P22: costs. Between 2010 and 2014, the share of doctors working in hospitals declined in Portugal (from
L905@P22: 55.7 to 49.8), while it increased in the euro area (from 47.9 to 54.9). However, the production mix in
L906@P22: the health sector may indicate remaining inefficiencies. The number of nurses has converged to the
L907@P22: euro area average but remains comparatively low. As a result, the ratio of nurses per physician is
L908@P22: significantly below the euro area average (1.5 and 2.3, respectively), leading to a costlier input mix.
L909@P22: Structural health indicators mostly point to higher efficiency in public hospitals and in
L910@P22: pharmaceutical spending (Figure 6)

L942@P23: 8. Since 2014, efforts to rationalize public compensation and employment have made
L943@P23: little progress. In 2016, the government gradually reversed the remaining wage cuts (80 percent)
L944@P23: adopted under the adjustment program (at a total cost of 0.3 percent of GDP),5 and returned to the
L945@P23: 35-hour week for a large share of the civil service. Some structural reforms have also been halted
L946@P23: and are unlikely to generate expected savings. The single wage scale was initially projected to save
L947@P23: about 0.4 percent of GDP by streamlining career paths. Savings (of about 0.1 percent of GDP) were
L948@P23: also expected from the adoption of the Single Supplements Scale through a reduction in the
L949@P23: number of supplements. However, the rolling out of these reforms has been postponed and will not
L950@P23: generate savings over the short and medium terms. Employment rationalization has fallen short of
L951@P23: the planned attrition (expected entry-to-exit ratio of 1:2), with an increase of public employment of
L952@P23: about 1.2 percent from end-2014 to end-2016. As a result, the wage bill has plateaued at
L953@P23: 11.3 percent of GDP since 2015, and is above the 2016 target set in the 2016-2020 Stability Program.
L954@P23: B. Challenges
L955@P23: 9. Portugal has set an ambitious consolidation path for the public wage bill over the next
L956@P23: four years, which needs to be supported by specific reforms. In the 2017-2021 Stability Program,
L957@P23: the wage bill is expected to decline from 11.3 percent of GDP in 2016 to 10.0 percent of GDP by
L958@P23: 2021. Even with more optimistic GDP growth assumptions, achieving an average annual reduction of
L959@P23: about 0.3 percent of GDP will require continuous expenditure savings which are not yet specified.
L960@P23: First, the objective of reducing public employment through attrition appears less ambitious, as it
L961@P23: only implies an entry-to-exit ratio of less than one, compared with a ratio of 1:3 during the
L962@P23: adjustment program, and 1:2 since then. Second, wage policies will be geared toward gradually
L963@P23: unfreezing career progression to reinforce staff motivation, with an expected fiscal impact of
L964@P23: +0.3 percent of GDP over 2017-2021. Finally, ensuring that public wages will not benefit from any
L965@P23: increase in the next four years might prove difficult in a context where private wages have started to
L966@P23: increase on the back of a cyclical upswing.
L967@P23: 10. Wage and public employment policies show evidence of procyclicality. The wage bill
L968@P23: experienced a larger decrease from 2011-2015 (-3.5 percent on average) than overall government
L969@P23: spending (-1.3 percent), followed by a sharp increase in the current cyclical upturn (+2.8 percent in
L970@P23: 2016) while total government spending continued to decline (-3.9 percent). Wage bill spending
L971@P23: tends therefore to exacerbate output fluctuations and weaken the stabilizing role of fiscal policy.
L972@P23: 11. Fiscal planning has suffered from numerous adjustments in government compensation
L973@P23: and employment policies. The government implemented a large array of short-term wage bill
L974@P23: consolidation measures that were then reversed, leading to difficulties in effectively integrating the
L975@P23: wage bill into budget planning. Thus, the wage bill was over executed in 2015-2016 (respectively
L976@P23: +1.5 and +1.2 percent), as estimating the fiscal impact of wage policy reversal proved difficult. The

L983@P24: 12. Portugal succeeded in reducing public employment, but further across-the-board
L984@P24: attrition may have an adverse impact on service provision in some sectors. Increasing the rate
L985@P24: of natural attrition would provide a gradual approach to rationalizing public employment, and
L986@P24: would generate savings in both the short and medium terms. While a similar level of attrition across
L987@P24: sectors would be easier to implement, it may have an adverse impact on service provision in some
L988@P24: sectors where staffing has already declined significantly.
L989@P24: 13. In the medium to long term, the main challenge for Portugal is to adjust employment
L990@P24: levels across sectors to demographic changes. Ageing will lead to higher needs in the health and
L991@P24: long-term care sectors, while the number of school-aged children will sharply fall in Portugal
L992@P24: (-20.8 percent from 2013-2030 projected in the 2015 Ageing Report, with 26.5 percent in primary
L993@P24: education). Adjusting service delivery in these areas will require careful workforce planning to ensure
L994@P24: the alignment of public employment levels with Portugal’s needs.
L995@P24: 14. Public sector employees in Portugal appear to benefit from a larger wage premium
L996@P24: than in most European countries. On average in the EU, public wages are higher than private
L997@P24: wages, even when controlling for skill differentials. However, Portugal has one of the highest publicprivate wage premiums in the EU (Figure 7), even though the data has significant lags as it refers to
L998@P24: pre-crisis level.6 More recent analysis point to a large albeit slightly declining public wage premium
L999@P24: in 2012 in Portugal (Perez and al., 2016), which remains above most EU countries (Campos and al.,
L1000@P24: 2015). In addition, the public wage premium still benefits both lower and higher income earners in
L1001@P24: Portugal, whereas in most other EU countries the later tend to have a negative wage premium.
L1002@P24: Finally, data for the education sector shows a higher ratio of primary teacher salary to per capita
L1003@P24: income than in other Europeans countries, another measure of relatively favorable compensation in
L1004@P24: the main public employment sector.
L1005@P24: 15. Portugal needs at the same time to continue improving skills in public administration.
L1006@P24: At present, lesser-qualified workers receive relatively high pay in the public sector compared to
L1007@P24: peers in the private sector as well as among more highly skilled civil servants. In addition, the wage
L1008@P24: grid is relatively flat and depends mostly on years of experience, rather than performance. This
L1009@P24: makes it difficult to attract highly qualified staff, because private sector opportunities (with lower
L1010@P24: entry salaries but steeper increases for performance) are considerably more attractive. To become
L1011@P24: more attractive, the civil service should identify specific jobs needed in the public sector (such as
L1012@P24: information technology experts) and revise the wage structure to offer competitive compensation.

L1024@P25: C. Policy Implications
L1025@P25: 16. To generate lasting fiscal savings, Portugal’s policy approach would need to move
L1026@P25: from across-the-board measures to deeper structural reforms. To achieve the sharp fiscal
L1027@P25: adjustment needed during the crisis, the authorities needed to resort to blunt but quick measures
L1028@P25: such as across-the-board attrition and temporary wage cuts. As in many advanced countries, such
L1029@P25: measures to reduce high wage bills proved successful in the short term, but could only be a
L1030@P25: temporary fix. Wage measures were gradually unwound and employment measures were diluted, as
L1031@P25: they proved difficult to sustain over the medium term. Reform fatigue led the government to
L1032@P25: suspend the implementation of structural pay policy reforms prepared during the adjustment
L1033@P25: program that aimed to generate durable savings. More recently though, the ongoing spending
L1034@P25: review created financial incentives for staff who identifies saving measures. Going forward, the
L1035@P25: recurrence of wage bill pressures associated with the unfreezing of career progression will require
L1036@P25: implementing structural reforms for more sustained wage bill adjustment.
L1037@P25: 17. Employment measures should rely on public sector restructuring to support staffing
L1038@P25: reallocation across sectors. Employment levels should be gradually aligned to future needs in key
L1039@P25: sectors, with a decrease in the education sector, and an increase in health sector in response to
L1040@P25: ageing. Some advanced countries have embarked on ambitious public sector restructuring to reduce
L1041@P25: public employment permanently while improving service delivery (IMF, 2016a). This approach relies
L1042@P25: on a functional review of the public sector to identify sectors where government employment can
L1043@P25: be reduced without adversely affecting service delivery, and an employee reallocation program. For
L1044@P25: example, reducing the number of teachers in the medium-term to align it with the expected decline
L1045@P25: in age-school population will require further restructuring of the school network. Consolidating

L1098@P26: 18. Containing public compensation will require structural wage measures. First, Portugal
L1099@P26: should develop comparisons between public and private sector wages to help inform wage
L1100@P26: negotiations. Some advanced economies conduct ad-hoc or regular comparisons to ensure that
L1101@P26: public-private sector wage differentials are contained or reduced. These benchmarking exercises
L1102@P26: should adopt a comprehensive approach of all factors that affect compensation level, including
L1103@P26: nonwage pay such as pensions and greater job security (IMF, 2016b). Second, wage increases and
L1104@P26: career progression mechanisms should reflect improvements in productivity. Third, efforts to
L1105@P26: streamlining non-wage compensation should be relaunched to reduce inequities among civil

L1120@P28: THE YOUTH IN PORTUGAL THROUGH THE CRISIS1
L1121@P28: Inequality and poverty in Europe during the financial crisis has received widespread attention, but
L1122@P28: somewhat less discussed has been the social impact of the crisis across generations. In a context where
L1123@P28: Portugal’s convergence toward lower European poverty and inequality standards has stalled over the
L1124@P28: last five years, the youth (aged 15-24 years) were especially affected by the downturn and adverse
L1125@P28: labor market developments.2 Their income has not yet fully recovered to pre-crisis levels, and their risk
L1126@P28: of poverty is the highest of all age groups. The youth are disproportionally unemployed or in
L1127@P28: precarious forms of employment in the context of strong market duality. The social security system has
L1128@P28: better protected the elderly from the impact of the crisis, with the youth less well covered against
L1129@P28: unemployment and poverty risks. Going forward, policies should focus on further reducing labor
L1130@P28: market duality to improve job prospects for young adults, and rebalancing fiscal redistribution to
L1131@P28: combat poverty in young adults.
L1132@P28: A. Rising Overall Inequality and Poverty in Portugal During the Crisis
L1133@P28: 1. The recent crisis affected both market inequality and income in Portugal (Figure 1). As
L1134@P28: measured by the Gini index, market inequality (before taxes and transfers) rose more in Portugal
L1135@P28: (+4.3 ppts) from 2009-2013 and is above the European average (OECD countries) and most peers.
L1136@P28: Median net income before social transfers largely declined (-14.1 percent) over 2009-2014, and
L1137@P28: underperformed European average, with Spain being the hardest hit among comparators
L1138@P28: (-24.1 percent).
L1139@P28: 2. Inequality after social transfers and taxes remains high in Portugal per European
L1140@P28: standards, as the crisis halted a long term declining trend. Both the Gini index and income
